title.en: Separable verbs: prefixes that wait until the very end

summary.en: Everyday verbs like aufmachen, aufwachen, and mitnehmen split to frame the whole clause.

body.en:
From season 1, episodes 1, 4 and 5.

When the gate bell rings at night, Werner says we *machen* *die Tür* together *auf* (from *aufmachen*, to open). Later he warns that room four *wacht* at quarter past seven *auf* (*aufwachen*, to wake up), and Klara realises two train passengers *nahmen* each other's suitcase *mit* (*mitnehmen*, to take along).

Many expressive German verbs pair a core verb (*machen*, *nehmen*, or phone-calling *anrufen*) with a stressed directional prefix such as *auf* or *mit*. In a present or simple-past main clause, the conjugated stem stays in slot two while the prefix travels all the way to the end of the clause.

That final prefix can completely flip the meaning (*aufmachen* opens a door while its twin closes it), so German listeners always stay tuned to the last word!

On replay, follow the bracket from *machen*, *wacht*, and *nahmen* out to the stressed *auf* and *mit* at the end.
